proposal.sql:
SELECT c.Segment, COUNT(*) AS JobCount, SUM(j.ContractValue) AS ContractValue
FROM reporting.vJobs AS j
JOIN reporting.vCustomers AS c ON j.CustomerId = c.CustomerId
GROUP BY c.Segment
ORDER BY c.Segment

outcomes.validated_sql:
SELECT
  [c].[segment] AS [segment],
  COUNT(*) AS [jobcount],
  SUM([j].[contractvalue]) AS [contractvalue]
FROM [reporting].[vjobs] AS [j]
JOIN [reporting].[vcustomers] AS [c]
  ON [j].[customerid] = [c].[customerid]
GROUP BY
  [c].[segment]
ORDER BY
  [segment]
outcomes.explanation: The query returned 3 rows with segment, jobcount, contractvalue. The complete bounded result is shown below; financial amounts use CAD.

learning.grain: vCustomers: one row per customer; vJobs: one row per job
explanation: Logical processing begins with FROM/JOIN, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT/window calculations, ORDER BY and TOP. The optimizer may execute differently.

The approved join preserves job grain: each job matches at most one customer, or one invoice ranked by ROW_NUMBER per JobId with rank = 1 in ON. LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched jobs with NULL values on the right.
GROUP BY produces one row per combination of grouping values.
Aggregates operate at the input grain. Margin percentage is a ratio of totals, not an average of job percentages.
cautions: Joining invoice and expense detail multiplies amounts; pre-aggregate each fact by JobId.
Budget variance = budget minus expenses; positive is favorable. Currency is CAD.
Avoid functions on indexed filter columns when a date range can express the filter.
Valid and authorized SQL can still answer the wrong business question; inspect grain and filters. Practice uses an independent reference, not the generated proposal.
